title: Communication Through Removable Media
summary: Communication through removable media is a dead-drop style channel in which two compromised hosts that cannot reach each other over the network exchange commands and files by writing them to a shared removable device. Typically the internet-connected host holds the adversary's real access, while a second host on a segmented or air-gapped network is compromised separately, often through replication by removable media. The implant on the isolated side copies output, tasking or collected files into a hidden directory on the drive; when the drive is carried back to a connected machine, the other implant reads that content and relays it outward, returning new instructions in the same place. The pattern leaves a physical artefact rather than network traffic: recurring file creation and modification on removable volumes, files with hidden or system attributes, unusual directories at the volume root, and a stable file naming or timestamp pattern that repeats each time the medium is mounted. Because there is no session to inspect, detection depends on correlating file-system auditing on the mount point with device connection records.

beginner.definition: Communication through removable media means two infected computers talk to each other by leaving messages on the same USB stick. One computer is on the internet, the other is locked away on a closed network. The attacker writes a command to the drive, and the other machine reads it later and writes back its answer.
beginner.whyItMatters: It gives an attacker a way to give orders inside a network that has no internet connection at all. There is no network traffic to watch, so normal monitoring sees nothing unusual. Without file monitoring on removable drives, an intrusion on an isolated network can stay hidden for a long time.
howItWorks: The attacker first infects a machine that does have a normal internet connection.
A second machine on the closed network is infected when the same drive is plugged into it.
The implant on the connected machine writes a command file onto the removable drive.
The drive is carried to the closed network and the second implant reads that command file.
The second implant writes results or stolen files back onto the same drive.
When the drive returns to the connected machine, those results are sent out to the attacker.
beginner.example: Think of two prisoners in different cells who cannot speak to each other. A cleaner wheels a laundry cart between the cells. One prisoner hides a note inside a folded towel, and the other prisoner finds it and hides a reply in the same place. Nobody ever saw the two of them communicate, yet messages travel both ways every day.
takeaways: This technique uses no network connection, so network monitoring alone will never find it.
Audit file creation and modification on removable volumes, not just device insertions.
Hidden files and folders at the top level of a USB drive deserve a closer look.

objectives: Explain how two compromised hosts can exchange commands without any network path between them.
Describe why this technique is used against segmented or air-gapped networks.
Identify file system and device connection artefacts that indicate a removable media channel.
Explain how this technique relates to replication through removable media as the delivery step.
List the monitoring sources needed to detect file activity on removable volumes.
